title: What is an investment thesis — and why does it matter?

blocks.html: When you start investing, especially in early-stage companies, it is very easy to be pulled in many directions.

A charismatic founder.
A hot market.
A compelling deck.
A friend investing.
A fear of missing out.
That is exactly why having an investment thesis matters.
An investment thesis is your own clear view on what you want to invest in, why it matters, and what you believe will drive long-term value.
It does not need to be over-engineered. But it does need to help you make better decisions.
At its simplest, your thesis should help you answer:

blocks.text: What do I believe is worth backing — and why?

blocks.html: That might be a sector, such as climate, health, education or future of work. It might be a type of founder. It might be a problem you believe is underfunded, misunderstood or becoming more urgent.
A good investment thesis helps you:

• stay aligned with your values and areas of interest;
  • filter opportunities more effectively;
  • avoid purely reactive or emotional decisions;
  • build conviction beyond the hype;
  • explain clearly why a deal does, or does not, fit.
This is particularly important in angel investing, where companies are early, information is limited, and the range of possible opportunities can feel overwhelming.

blocks.text: How to start building your investment thesis

blocks.html: Start with your focus.

What sectors, themes or problems do you genuinely care about? Where do you have experience, networks or curiosity? This could be women’s health, climate adaptation, inclusive finance, education, social mobility, or any area where you believe innovation and capital can make a difference.
Then understand the landscape.
Who is building in this space? What trends are driving change? Where are the gaps? What is broken in the current system? Which solutions are gaining traction, and which ones are struggling?
Look closely at individual companies.

Is the founder solving a real and urgent problem? Is the product differentiated? Is there evidence of demand? Does the team understand the customer? Is there a credible route to scale? And, if impact matters to you, is the impact embedded in the business model rather than added as a nice-to-have?
Write down your beliefs.
What do you believe about this market? Why now? Why this solution? Why this team? What would need to be true for this to become a strong investment?
Also write down the risks.
A thesis is not only about what excites you. It should also make you more honest about what could go wrong: market timing, regulation, customer adoption, competition, execution, or funding risk.
Then test it.
Speak to founders, operators, investors, advisors and people with lived experience of the problem. Look for evidence that supports your view, but also pay attention to what challenges it.
And keep refining.

Your thesis should evolve as you learn. The point is not to lock yourself into a rigid view forever. The point is to build a disciplined way of thinking, so that each investment teaches you something and makes your next decision stronger.
Finally, document it.
It does not need to be a long report. A few clear paragraphs are enough. What matters is that it captures your intention, your reasoning and your decision-making criteria.
Your investment thesis does not need to be perfect.
But it should be yours.
It is a practical tool to help you invest with more clarity, more discipline and more purpose — and to avoid being carried away by whatever happens to be loudest in the market.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of an investment thesis?

options.text: To guarantee a financial return
To help investors decide what to back, why it matters, and what fits their goals
To follow what other investors are doing
To avoid doing due diligence

quiz.q: Why is an investment thesis especially useful in angel investing?

options.text: Because early-stage opportunities often come with limited information and high uncertainty
Because all startups are easy to compare
Because angel investors do not need to assess risk
Because it removes the need to speak to founders

quiz.q: Which of the following should an investor consider when building their thesis?

options.text: Their values, interests, knowledge and networks
Only what is trending on LinkedIn
Only what their friends are investing in
Only companies with the most polished pitch deck

quiz.q: A strong investment thesis should help an investor avoid:

options.text: Thinking about risks
Asking questions
Reactive or emotional investment decisions
Learning from other investors

quiz.q: True or false: An investment thesis should never change once it has been written.

options.text: True
False

quiz.explanation: A strong thesis should evolve as you learn, see more companies, understand markets better, and reflect on your investment decisions.

blocks.text: Deal Sourcing: Where Do Angel Investors Find Opportunities?

blocks.html: Before you can screen startups, you need to find them.

Deal sourcing is simply the process of identifying investment opportunities. For angel investors, this can happen in many ways, and the quality of your deal flow will often depend on the strength and relevance of your network.
There is no single “right” way to source deals. The key is to be intentional and to build access to opportunities that fit your investment thesis.
Joining an angel network or syndicate can be one of the easiest ways to start seeing curated opportunities.
These groups often provide access to founder pitches, deal memos, due diligence discussions and shared learning with other investors.
This can be particularly useful for new angels because you are not reviewing deals in isolation. You can learn from how others ask questions, assess risk and build conviction.
Some of the strongest opportunities come through trusted referrals.
This might be from other founders, operators, investors, advisors or people in your professional network.
The benefit of referrals is that they often come with some context. But it is still important to do your own work. A warm introduction is not the same as investment validation.
Accelerators, incubators and venture builders can be useful sources of early-stage companies.

Demo days can provide a quick view of multiple startups in a short period of time. They can also help investors identify emerging themes, founder talent and sectors where innovation is happening quickly.
However, demo day pitches are designed to be compelling. They are a starting point, not a substitute for due diligence.
If you have a specific investment thesis, sector communities can be a powerful source of deal flow.

For example, if you are interested in healthtech, climate, fintech, education or future of work, you can spend time in the communities where founders, operators and experts in those sectors are already active.
This might include industry events, specialist newsletters, LinkedIn communities, academic spinout networks, professional associations or founder groups.
The more specific your thesis, the easier it becomes to know where to look.
Building relationships with other angels is one of the best ways to improve both the quantity and quality of your deal flow.
Other investors may share opportunities, invite you into syndicates, or ask you to look at deals where your expertise is relevant.
This is also useful from a learning perspective. Seeing how different investors think about the same opportunity can sharpen your own judgement.
Sometimes investors proactively reach out to founders they find interesting.
This could be after reading about a company, seeing a founder speak at an event, following their work online, or identifying a startup in a sector that fits their thesis.
This approach requires more effort, but it can help you build relationships before a formal fundraising process starts.
Your existing network can also be a source of deal flow.
Colleagues, clients, advisors, lawyers, accountants, consultants, board members and operators may all come across early-stage companies.
The important thing is to be clear about what you are interested in. If people understand your investment thesis, they are more likely to send relevant opportunities your way.
There are also online platforms where startups raise capital and angel investors can review opportunities.
These can provide access to a broad range of deals, sometimes with lower minimum ticket sizes.
However, investors should still be selective. More access does not automatically mean better opportunities. The same screening discipline applies.

blocks.text: How to Screen an Early-Stage Startup

blocks.html: Once you have started to develop your investment thesis, the next question is: how do you actually assess a startup opportunity?
At angel stage, there is rarely a perfect answer. Companies are young. Information is limited. The numbers may be early, incomplete or still evolving.
That is why a structured screening framework is helpful.

It does not replace judgement, instinct or experience. But it gives you a disciplined way to look at each opportunity, compare companies more consistently, and avoid being overly influenced by a polished pitch, a charismatic founder or market hype.
Below is an 8-point framework angel investors can use when reviewing early-stage startups.
This is about understanding whether the startup is solving a real, painful and important problem.
A product can look impressive, but if the problem is not urgent enough, customers may not pay for it, use it, or change their behaviour.
Ask yourself:

• What problem is the company solving?
  • Who has this problem, and how painful is it?
  • Is the problem frequent, urgent or expensive enough to justify a new solution?
  • Is there evidence that customers care?
  • Has the product changed based on customer feedback?
  • What makes this solution better than what already exists?
At early stage, I would rather see a simple product solving a real problem than a sophisticated product looking for a market.
A strong startup needs more than a good product. It also needs a market that is large enough, growing enough, or underserved enough to support meaningful scale.

This does not always mean the company needs to operate in a huge market from day one. Some of the best businesses start in a specific niche. But there should be a credible path to a bigger opportunity over time.
Ask yourself:

• Who is the target customer?
  • How big is the addressable market?
  • Is the market growing, changing or being disrupted?
  • Are there underserved customer segments?
  • Is this a crowded space, or is there room for a differentiated player?
  • What market trends support this opportunity?
The key question is not just “is this a big market?” but “can this company realistically capture a meaningful part of it?”
Timing matters more than we sometimes admit.
Some ideas fail because they are too early. Others arrive just as regulation, technology, customer behaviour or market conditions are shifting in their favour.
Ask yourself:

• Why is now the right time for this solution?
  • What has changed in the market?
  • Are there regulatory, technological, social or economic tailwinds?
  • Have similar solutions failed before? If so, why?
  • Are customers ready to adopt this now?
A great idea at the wrong time can still be a poor investment.
Unit economics help you understand whether the business can make money as it grows.

At very early stage, the numbers may not yet be fully proven. But founders should still understand the basic economics of their model: how much it costs to acquire and serve a customer, how much revenue that customer can generate, and whether the margins can improve over time.
Ask yourself:

• What is the revenue model?
  • What is the customer acquisition cost?
  • What is the expected lifetime value of a customer?
  • Are gross margins attractive?
  • What needs to happen for the business to become profitable?
  • Do the economics improve with scale?
You do not need perfect numbers at pre-seed or seed stage. But you do need to see that the founder understands the economic engine of the business.
Scalability is about whether the business can grow without costs increasing at the same pace.
Some businesses require heavy manual work, customisation or headcount to grow. Others have the potential to expand more efficiently through technology, partnerships, networks or repeatable processes.
Ask yourself:

• Can this model scale beyond the first few customers?
  • What are the operational bottlenecks?
  • Does growth rely heavily on hiring more people?
  • Can the product, service or platform be replicated efficiently?
  • Are systems and processes being built with scale in mind?
  • What would need to be true for the company to grow 10x?
A business does not need to be fully scalable from day one, but the founder should have a credible view of how scalability will be achieved.
Defensibility is what allows a startup to protect its position over time.
If the idea works, others may copy it. Larger players may enter the market. Competitors may try to win on price, speed or distribution.
Ask yourself:

• What makes this company difficult to copy?
  • Does it have proprietary technology, data or intellectual property?
  • Are there regulatory advantages or specialist knowledge?
  • Are there network effects?
  • Are switching costs high for customers?
  • Is the brand, community or distribution strategy distinctive?
Not every early-stage company will have deep defensibility from the start. But there should be a credible path to building it.
Angel investors usually make returns when there is a liquidity event, such as an acquisition, secondary sale or IPO.
That means it is important to understand who might eventually buy the company, why they would buy it, and what milestones would make the business attractive.
Ask yourself:

• What are the most likely exit routes?
  • Who could be a potential acquirer?
  • Why would this company be strategically valuable to them?
  • Are there comparable exits in the sector?
  • What milestones would increase exit potential?
  • Is the company building something that could attract later-stage investors or strategic buyers?
At angel stage, exits are uncertain. But they should not be ignored.
At early stage, the team is often the most important factor.

The product may change. The market entry strategy may change. The business model may evolve. What matters is whether the founders have the capability, resilience and judgement to keep learning and executing.
Ask yourself:

• Why is this the right team to solve this problem?
  • Do they understand the market and the customer?
  • Are they fully committed?
  • Do they have complementary skills?
  • Are there any obvious gaps in the team?
  • How do they respond to challenge, feedback or setbacks?
  • Do they show coachability without losing conviction?
For me, this is often where a lot of the judgement sits. You are backing people as much as you are backing a product.
Not every criterion will carry the same weight at every stage.
For very early-stage companies, the most important areas are often:

• the quality and commitment of the team;
  • the strength of the problem being solved;
  • the timing of the opportunity;
  • early signs of customer validation.
For later-stage companies, investors may place more emphasis on:

• unit economics;
  • scalability;
  • revenue traction;
  • competitive positioning;
  • exit potential.
The framework is not a rigid scoring tool. It is a way to structure your thinking and make sure you are asking the right questions.

blocks.text: A Note on Bias and Discipline

blocks.html: Angel investing is human. That means bias can easily enter the process.

You may like a founder because they remind you of someone. You may be influenced by who else is investing. You may feel pressure to move quickly because a round is “closing soon”. You may over-index on a polished pitch or underestimate a founder who does not fit the usual pattern.
A framework helps create some discipline.
It can help you pause and ask:

• Am I excited because this is genuinely compelling, or because everyone else seems excited?
  • Am I making assumptions about the founder, the market or the customer?
  • Have I looked at the risks as carefully as the upside?
  • Have I asked someone with relevant expertise to challenge my thinking?
This does not mean removing instinct entirely. It means making sure instinct is supported by evidence, analysis and reflection.

Waiting for startups to appear without building any network
Investing only because a friend invested

quiz.q: True or false: A screening framework removes all risk from angel investing.

options.text: True
False

quiz.explanation: A framework does not remove risk. It helps investors understand the risk they are taking, why they are taking it, and whether the opportunity fits their thesis and return expectations.

blocks.html: Investing in an early-stage company inevitably involves uncertainty. At the pre-seed stage, the business may have limited revenue, an unfinished product and only a small amount of customer data. The investment decision therefore cannot be based on a long trading history or extensive financial records. Instead, investors must assess the quality of the evidence available, identify what remains unproven and decide whether the potential return justifies the risks.

Due diligence is the process of investigating and validating the information provided by the founders before making an investment. It involves looking beyond the pitch deck to understand whether the company exists as described, whether the founders can credibly execute their plans and whether the proposed investment terms properly reflect the opportunity and its risks.

Due diligence is not intended to remove all uncertainty—this is impossible in angel investing. Its purpose is to help investors make a more informed and disciplined decision. A compelling founder and an exciting presentation may generate interest, but due diligence tests whether the underlying facts support the investment case.
It can help an investor to:

• Verify the claims made in the pitch deck and during conversations with the founders.
  • Understand the company’s ownership, finances and legal position.
  • Assess the strength and commitment of the founding team.
  • Validate the problem, product, market opportunity and early customer demand.
  • Identify material risks, inconsistencies or unanswered questions.
  • Confirm that the proposed valuation and investment terms are reasonable.
  • Establish whether the founders are transparent, organised and receptive to challenge.

blocks.text: The Challenges of Pre-Seed Due Diligence

blocks.html: Conducting due diligence on a pre-seed company requires judgement. Many of the documents and metrics available for a mature business will not yet exist. Financial forecasts are based largely on assumptions, customer traction may be limited and the product itself may still be evolving.

This does not mean that due diligence should be less rigorous. It means that it should be proportionate to the company’s stage. Investors should not expect a pre-seed startup to operate like an established company, but they should expect the founders to understand their business, explain their assumptions and be honest about what has—and has not—yet been proven.
Some of the most common challenges include:

• Limited financial and operating history.
  • Forecasts based on assumptions rather than established revenue.
  • Incomplete legal, governance or employment documentation.
  • Uncertainty over market size and customer demand.
  • Technology or intellectual property that has not yet been fully tested.
  • Key-person risk, particularly where the business relies heavily on one founder.
  • Limited time and resources available to individual angel investors.
  • The risk of becoming influenced by excitement, personal connection or fear of missing out.

Due diligence therefore provides structure without replacing judgement. The objective is not simply to collect documents, but to understand what they demonstrate, what questions they raise and whether the overall story remains coherent when tested.
Due Diligence Document Checklist for Pre-Seed Startups

The following documents can help investors validate a startup’s potential. Not every document will exist at the pre-seed stage, and the level of detail should be proportionate to the company’s maturity. Where information is not yet available, founders should be able to explain why and how they intend to address the gap.
1. Corporate and Financial Documents

• Certificate of Incorporation: Confirmation that the company has been legally established.
  • Articles of Association: The rules governing how the company is owned and managed.
  • Capitalisation Table: A current record of shareholders, ownership percentages, share classes, options and other rights to acquire shares.
  • Initial Budget or Financial Projections: Forecast revenue, expenditure and cash requirements for the next 12–24 months.
  • Cash Position and Burn Rate: Where relevant, details of the company’s available cash and expected monthly spending.
  • Use of Funds: An explanation of how the investment being raised will be used and the milestones it is expected to achieve.
2. Legal Documents

• Intellectual Property Documentation: Details of patents, trademarks, registered designs, proprietary software or other technology owned or used by the company.
  • IP Assignment Agreements: Evidence that intellectual property created by founders, employees or contractors belongs to the company.
  • Customer Contracts or Letters of Intent: Evidence of commercial interest, pilots, early sales or expected future business.
  • Partnership Agreements, Memoranda of Understanding or Contracts: Agreements with suppliers, customers, distributors or strategic collaborators.
  • Details of Pending or Previous Legal Issues: Information about any disputes, claims, regulatory matters or threatened legal action.
  • Data Protection and Regulatory Documentation: Where relevant, evidence that the company understands the regulations applying to its product, customers and use of data.
3. Product and Technology Documents

• Product Roadmap: Planned product development and key milestones for the next 6–12 months.
  • Prototype or Minimum Viable Product: Access to a working version, demonstration or other evidence of the product’s development.
  • Technology Overview: An explanation of how the product works, its principal components and its technical differentiation.
  • Third-Party Partnerships and Integrations: Details of important technology providers, platforms, licences or integrations on which the product depends.
  • Trial Results and Quantified Metrics: Data from testing, pilots or product trials, including engagement, retention or performance indicators.
  • Scalability Plans: An explanation of how the product and its supporting infrastructure can accommodate increasing customer demand.
  • Research, Articles and Publications: Independent research, technical papers or media coverage that may help validate the technology, intellectual property or market opportunity.
4. Market and Customer Validation

• Customer Testimonials or Beta-User Feedback: Evidence of how potential or existing customers experience and value the product.
  • Sales Pipeline and Conversion Metrics: Details of prospective customers and their progress through the sales process.
  • Market Research: Surveys, interviews, focus groups or third-party reports supporting the need for the product.
  • Customer Acquisition Channels: The channels the company intends to test or develop over the next six months.
  • Go-to-Market Strategy: The plan for launching and selling the product, including target customers, pricing, marketing and distribution.
  • Customer Feedback: Findings from user interviews, surveys, pilots or beta testing, including how the product has evolved in response.
  • Customer Order Book: Confirmed orders, contracts or other evidence of committed demand, where available.
5. Team Documents

• Founder and Team CVs or Biographies: Evidence of relevant experience, capabilities and sector knowledge.
  • Roles and Responsibilities: Clarity on how responsibilities are divided across the founding team.
  • Employment, Consultancy or Contractor Agreements: Documentation covering the people working for the company.
  • Time Commitment: Confirmation of whether each founder is working full-time or part-time and when any part-time founder intends to transition.
  • Founder and Employee Incentives: Details of salaries, equity ownership, share options and other financial incentives.
  • Recruitment Plan: Key roles the company expects to hire and how these hires relate to the proposed use of investment funds.
  • References: Where appropriate, references from previous employers, colleagues, investors, customers or business partners.
6. Ownership and Fundraising Documents

• Previous Funding Documents: Agreements relating to earlier angel investment, founder funding, grants, convertible instruments or other sources of capital.
  • Shareholders’ Agreement: The agreement setting out the rights and obligations of the company’s shareholders, where one is already in place.
  • Current Capitalisation Table: Including all issued shares, options, convertible instruments and other rights that could affect future ownership.
  • Detailed Fundraising History: The amounts previously raised, dates, valuations, investors and instruments used.
  • Current Investment Terms: The proposed valuation, share class, investor rights and other terms applying to the present round.
  • Tax-Relief Documentation: For UK investments, any available information relating to advance assurance or eligibility for SEIS or EIS.

The presence of these documents does not, on its own, make a company investable. Investors should consider whether the information is accurate, consistent and supported by evidence. They should also pay attention to how founders respond when information is questioned. Transparency, preparation and a willingness to acknowledge uncertainty can be as revealing as the documents themselves.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of due diligence when considering an angel investment?

options.text: To eliminate all risks associated with the investment
To verify the founders’ claims and make a more informed investment decision
To guarantee that the startup will become profitable
To negotiate the lowest possible valuation

quiz.explanation: Due diligence cannot eliminate the uncertainty of angel investing. It helps investors validate the information provided, identify material risks and make a more informed decision.

quiz.q: How should an investor approach due diligence on a pre-seed startup?

options.text: Expect the same documentation and financial history as an established company
Focus only on the founders’ previous experience
Conduct due diligence proportionate to the company’s stage
Avoid due diligence because there will be insufficient information

quiz.explanation: A pre-seed company may have limited revenue, customer data and operating history. Due diligence should remain rigorous but reflect the company’s early stage.

quiz.q: What does a capitalisation table—or cap table—show?

options.text: The startup’s expected revenue and expenditure
The company’s customer acquisition strategy
The company’s ownership structure, share classes, options and convertible instruments
The founders’ professional qualifications

quiz.explanation: The cap table helps investors understand who owns the company and how existing options, share classes or convertible instruments could affect future ownership.

quiz.q: Which document provides evidence that intellectual property created by founders, employees or contractors belongs to the company?

options.text: A product roadmap
An IP assignment agreement
A letter of intent
A financial projection

quiz.explanation: An IP assignment agreement confirms that relevant intellectual property has been legally transferred to the company rather than remaining personally owned by an individual founder, employee or contractor.

quiz.q: If a pre-seed startup cannot provide every document requested during due diligence, what should an investor expect?

options.text: The investment should automatically be rejected
The founder should create documents containing estimated information
The founder should explain why the information is unavailable and how the gap will be addressed
The investor should ignore the missing information

quiz.explanation: Not every document will exist at the pre-seed stage. However, founders should be transparent about what is missing, explain why and demonstrate how they intend to address the gap.

title: Understanding EIS and SEIS tax reliefs

blocks.html: Investing in an early-stage company can generate significant returns, but it also involves considerable risk. Many startups fail, investments are usually illiquid, and investors may need to wait several years before seeing a return—if one materialises at all.
To encourage individuals to provide capital to young, high-growth businesses, the UK Government introduced two tax-advantaged investment schemes:

• The Seed Enterprise Investment Scheme (SEIS)
  • The Enterprise Investment Scheme (EIS)

Both schemes offer valuable tax reliefs to eligible UK taxpayers who invest in qualifying companies. These reliefs can reduce the initial cost of an investment, protect part of the investor’s downside if the company fails, and allow successful investments to generate tax-free capital gains.

However, tax relief should never be the main reason for making an investment. A weak company does not become a good investment simply because it qualifies for SEIS or EIS. The fundamentals—team, product, market, business model, valuation and potential returns—must still support the investment decision.

Early-stage companies are important contributors to innovation, employment and economic growth. However, they often find it difficult to raise funding because they have limited trading history, few assets and a higher probability of failure.

SEIS and EIS help compensate investors for accepting this additional risk. In simple terms, the Government shares some of the risk by offering tax incentives to individuals prepared to invest their capital in qualifying businesses.
The schemes benefit both sides of the investment:

• Startups become more attractive to potential investors.
  • Investors receive some protection against the risks of early-stage investing.
  • More private capital is directed towards innovative UK businesses.

blocks.text: What is the difference between SEIS and EIS?

blocks.html: SEIS is primarily designed for very young companies at the beginning of their journey. EIS supports somewhat more established businesses seeking capital to grow.

rows: Maximum annual investment qualifying for relief
Up to £2 million if at least £1 million is invested in knowledge-intensive companies
Usually tax-free if the conditions are met
Usually tax-free if the conditions are met
Relief connected to reinvesting an existing capital gain
50% of the qualifying amount may be exempt

blocks.html: These are investor limits. Separate limits and eligibility requirements apply to the company receiving the investment. For example, a company can currently raise a maximum of £250,000 through SEIS.
The most immediate benefit is a reduction in the investor’s Income Tax liability.
An investor can claim Income Tax relief equal to 50% of the amount invested.
For example:

• You invest £10,000 in an SEIS-qualifying company.
  • You may claim £5,000 in Income Tax relief.
  • The initial net cost of the investment is therefore £5,000.
An investor can claim Income Tax relief equal to 30% of the amount invested.
For example:

• You invest £10,000 in an EIS-qualifying company.
  • You may claim £3,000 in Income Tax relief.
  • The initial net cost of the investment is therefore £7,000.

The relief cannot exceed the amount of UK Income Tax the investor owes. If your Income Tax liability is only £2,000, for example, you cannot use a £5,000 SEIS relief to generate an additional £3,000 payment from HMRC.

Investors can generally claim the relief in the tax year in which the shares are issued or elect to carry it back to the previous tax year, subject to the relevant annual limits and sufficient Income Tax liability.

blocks.text: 2. Tax-free capital gains on the investment

blocks.html: If the company succeeds and the shares increase in value, any gain made when qualifying SEIS or EIS shares are sold will normally be exempt from Capital Gains Tax.
To benefit, the investor must generally:

• have received Income Tax relief on the investment;
  • retain that relief;
  • hold the shares for at least three years; and
  • continue to meet the scheme’s conditions.
For example:

• You invest £10,000 in a qualifying company.
  • Several years later, you sell the shares for £50,000.
  • The £40,000 gain may be free from Capital Gains Tax.
This can make a considerable difference to the overall return from a successful angel investment.
Dividends, however, are not tax-free under EIS or SEIS. In practice, early-stage companies rarely pay dividends because they normally reinvest available cash into growth.

Not every startup investment will succeed. If an SEIS or EIS investment is sold at a loss—or the shares become of negligible value—the investor may be able to offset the remaining loss against their taxable income or capital gains.
The loss is calculated after deducting any Income Tax relief already received.
Assume an additional-rate taxpayer invests £10,000 in an EIS company and the company fails completely:

• Original investment: £10,000
  • EIS Income Tax relief: £3,000
  • Remaining amount at risk: £7,000
  • Potential loss relief at a 45% tax rate: £3,150
  • Effective net loss: £3,850
If the same investor makes a £10,000 SEIS investment:

• Original investment: £10,000
  • SEIS Income Tax relief: £5,000
  • Remaining amount at risk: £5,000
  • Potential loss relief at a 45% tax rate: £2,250
  • Effective net loss: £2,750

These examples assume the investment becomes completely worthless, the investor has sufficient taxable income, and all relevant conditions are met. The actual relief depends on the investor’s circumstances and marginal tax rate.
Loss relief reduces the financial impact of a failed investment, but it does not eliminate it. The investor still loses money.

blocks.text: 4. Capital Gains Tax reinvestment relief under SEIS

blocks.html: SEIS provides an additional benefit where an investor has made a taxable capital gain from selling another asset and reinvests that gain in qualifying SEIS shares.

An investor may be able to exempt from Capital Gains Tax an amount equal to 50% of the qualifying SEIS investment. Because investors can claim SEIS relief on investments of up to £200,000 per tax year, the maximum amount of gain that can potentially benefit from the exemption is £100,000.
For example:

• You make a taxable gain of £20,000 from selling an asset.
  • You invest £20,000 in qualifying SEIS shares within the relevant period.
  • You may be able to exempt £10,000—50% of the amount reinvested—from Capital Gains Tax.
SEIS reinvestment relief is an exemption rather than merely a delay in paying the tax, provided the conditions continue to be met.

blocks.text: 5. Capital Gains Tax deferral under EIS

blocks.html: EIS offers Capital Gains Tax deferral relief. If an investor makes a taxable gain from disposing of another asset and reinvests the gain in qualifying EIS shares, the Capital Gains Tax liability may be postponed.
The EIS investment must generally be made between:

• one year before the original gain arose; and
  • three years after the gain arose.

Unlike the SEIS exemption, the deferred gain does not normally disappear. It generally becomes taxable again when a triggering event occurs—for example, when the EIS shares are sold, redeemed or cease to qualify.
Deferral can still be valuable because it delays the tax payment and allows the investor to deploy more of their capital in the meantime.

blocks.text: What must an investor do to qualify?

blocks.html: The detailed rules are complex, but some of the main investor requirements include:

• The investment must normally be made in newly issued, fully paid shares.
  • The shares must generally be paid for in cash.
  • The shares must be genuinely at risk and cannot include arrangements designed to protect the investor’s capital.
  • The investor and their associates must not normally control more than 30% of the company.
  • The investor must generally hold the shares for at least three years.
  • The investor must not receive prohibited value or benefits from the company.
  • Particular restrictions apply to employees and paid directors, although some angel investors who become directors can still qualify.
The company must also continue to meet the relevant scheme conditions. An investor can lose relief because of something the company does after the investment, not only because of their own actions.

blocks.text: Advance assurance: useful, but not a guarantee

blocks.html: Many startups apply to HMRC for “advance assurance” before raising an SEIS or EIS round. This indicates that, based on the information provided, HMRC considers that the proposed investment is likely to meet certain scheme requirements.
Advance assurance can give investors greater confidence, but it is important to understand what it does—and does not—mean.
It is not:

• an endorsement of the company;
  • confirmation that the business is a good investment;
  • a substitute for due diligence; or
  • an unconditional guarantee that tax relief will be available.
Final eligibility depends on the investment being completed as described and the company and investor continuing to satisfy the applicable rules.

blocks.text: How does an investor claim the relief?

blocks.html: The company must first issue the shares and complete the required HMRC compliance process. Once HMRC authorises the company to do so, it provides the investor with an EIS3 or SEIS3 compliance certificate.
The investor can then claim the relief through their Self Assessment tax return or, depending on the circumstances, request an adjustment from HMRC.
Relief is not usually available immediately after transferring the money. There may be a delay while the company completes the required activities and obtains permission to issue the certificates.
Investors should retain:

• the EIS3 or SEIS3 certificate;
  • the share subscription agreement;
  • evidence of payment;
  • the share certificate or nominee statement;
  • details of the share issue date; and
  • any relevant correspondence with the company or investment platform.
SEIS and EIS are powerful tools for angel investors. They can reduce the upfront cost of investing, protect part of the downside and make successful exits more tax-efficient.
They should, however, be viewed as a risk mitigant—not as an investment strategy.
The right order is:

1. Decide whether the company is an attractive investment.
  2. Conduct appropriate due diligence.
  3. Assess whether the valuation and terms are reasonable.
  4. Confirm the expected SEIS or EIS eligibility.
  5. Consider how the relief applies to your personal tax position.
Never allow the availability of tax relief to turn an investment you would otherwise reject into one you are prepared to make.

This lesson is for educational purposes and does not constitute tax, legal or investment advice. Tax treatment depends on individual circumstances and may change. Investors should consult a suitably qualified tax adviser and review the latest HMRC guidance on venture capital scheme reliefs before investing. Further information on the company requirements is available in HMRC’s SEIS guidance and EIS guidance.

blocks.text: How to turn individual investments into a considered portfolio

blocks.html: The first few angel investments can feel like a series of separate decisions. You meet a founder, review a pitch, carry out due diligence and decide whether to write a cheque. But over time, those decisions add up. The question is no longer just, “Do I like this company?” It is also, “What role would this investment play in my portfolio?”

That shift matters because early-stage investing is uncertain. Even a promising business with a capable team can struggle to raise its next round, lose a major customer or take much longer than expected to reach profitability. Some investments may fail altogether. A small number may account for much of a portfolio's eventual return. You cannot know at the outset which companies will fall into which category.

Portfolio construction gives you a way to make decisions before the excitement or pressure of a particular deal takes over. It means deciding how much you can afford to commit, how many companies you hope to back, what size your initial cheques will be and how much capital you will keep available for later rounds. Diversification is one part of that plan. It helps reduce reliance on any single outcome, although it cannot remove the risk of losing money.

blocks.text: 1. Start with the amount you can afford to lose

blocks.html: Before deciding how many startups to invest in, decide how much of your overall wealth you are willing to put into high-risk, illiquid investments. Angel capital is money you should be able to leave invested for years, with no certainty about when, or whether, you will receive anything back.

The UK Financial Conduct Authority suggests putting no more than 10% of your total net assets into high-risk investments as a general rule of thumb. This is an upper guide for high-risk investments collectively, not an instruction to put 10% into startups. If you already own other high-risk assets, those exposures matter too. Your personal limit may be substantially lower. Do not count on an exit to pay for a known expense, and keep money needed for emergencies, debt commitments and near-term plans outside your angel budget. FCA guidance

• If every angel investment I made were written down to zero, would my finances still be secure?
  • How much can I commit without needing access to it for several years?
  • What other high-risk or illiquid investments do I already hold?
  • How much time can I realistically devote to sourcing, due diligence and keeping up with the companies?

Your investment budget is the total you are prepared to commit over the life of your plan. It includes future follow-on investments, platform or syndicate costs where applicable, and any commitments you have already made. It is not a target you must spend.

blocks.text: 2. Translate your investment thesis into portfolio rules

blocks.html: Your investment thesis, discussed earlier in this series, describes the kinds of founders and businesses you want to support and why. Your portfolio strategy puts numbers and boundaries around that intention.

You might focus on UK pre-seed businesses in health and sustainability because you understand those markets and have relevant networks. That is a starting point. Then ask: Will you invest only through a syndicate or also directly? What is the most you will commit to any one company? Will you include businesses outside your strongest sector to reduce concentration, or does that take you beyond your ability to assess them well?

There is no benefit in diversifying into businesses you do not understand simply to fill a category. Equally, investing in ten companies exposed to the same customer, regulatory change or funding market may leave you less diversified than the number suggests. Look beyond the labels: different sectors can share the same underlying risks.
Write down four objectives for your portfolio, such as:

1. Invest only money I can afford to lose and hold for the long term.
  2. Back companies that meet my stated thesis and pass a consistent due diligence process.
  3. Build exposure across several businesses, founders and sources of opportunity.
  4. Reserve capital for selective follow-on rounds without treating further investment as automatic.

You may also have non-financial objectives, such as supporting underrepresented founders or using your expertise to help a particular sector. Be clear about these alongside your financial goals. Neither removes the need to assess the investment on its merits.

blocks.text: 3. Plan the number and size of your initial investments

blocks.html: A single startup is a highly concentrated bet. Building a portfolio spreads exposure across companies whose outcomes will differ. Around 15–20 investments is often used as a working ambition for an angel portfolio; an experienced angel writing for the UK Business Angels Association argues that at least 20 are needed for reasonable diversification. It is a planning guide, not a threshold at which losses disappear, and many people will need to build towards it over several years. UKBAA perspective

Start with the arithmetic. Suppose you set aside £40,000 as your total angel budget. If you reserve half for later rounds, you have £20,000 for initial cheques. Across 20 companies, that would be £1,000 per company before any fees. If the opportunities available to you have a £5,000 minimum cheque, that particular plan does not work: four initial investments would use up the whole initial allocation. You would need to change the budget, timescale, ticket size or route to investing. A syndicate or pooled vehicle may make smaller exposures possible, but check its minimums, fees, deal terms and the decisions delegated to others.

The point is not to force 20 investments into your budget. It is to spot a mismatch before you start writing cheques. Fewer thoughtful investments can be a better starting point than a rushed attempt to reach a number. Just be honest about the concentration risk while your portfolio is small.

An initial ticket limit can also protect you from making an oversized first investment in the company you feel most excited about. The strongest presentation in your first month of investing is not necessarily the best opportunity you will see over the next three years.

blocks.text: 4. Keep some capital for follow-on rounds

blocks.html: Most growing startups need to raise capital more than once. A follow-on investment is an additional investment you make in a company you already back when it raises another round. Setting money aside gives you the option to participate if the company makes progress and the new round still looks attractive.

A simple starting model is 50% for initial investments and 50% reserved for follow-ons. On a £40,000 budget, that is £20,000 for new companies and £20,000 held back for possible later rounds. This split is a planning assumption, not a universal rule. The right reserve depends on the stage at which you invest, the likely future funding needs of your companies, your available cash and whether you want to make more initial investments instead.

Most importantly, a reserve is an option, not a promise to invest. Some companies will never raise again. Others will ask for more money without showing enough progress. You do not need to spread follow-on capital evenly across all your investments, and you should not put in more simply because you have already invested.
When a follow-on opportunity appears, ask:

• What did the company say it would achieve with the last round, and what has it actually achieved?
  • How much cash does it have, how quickly is it spending it and what milestone should this round fund?
  • Have the team, market opportunity, risks or terms changed?
  • At the proposed valuation, would I invest in this company today if I were seeing it for the first time?
  • How much exposure would I have to this one company after the new cheque?

You may decide to invest more in a company that has earned your conviction. You may also decline a follow-on and accept that your percentage ownership could fall as new shares are issued. That is a normal portfolio decision, not a failure of loyalty to the founder.
Diversification means more than reaching a company count. Consider several dimensions together:

rows: What share of my total angel budget would be tied to this one business, including follow-ons?
Would the same market shock affect several of my companies?
Am I taking similar product, customer and financing risks across every deal?
Are my companies exposed to the same local funding market or regulatory environment?
Am I investing everything during one period of valuations and market conditions?
Am I seeing deals through only one syndicate or network, with the same selection biases?

blocks.html: Investing over time, sometimes called pacing, can be as useful as spreading investments across sectors. It allows you to learn from early decisions, see different market conditions and avoid committing your full budget before you understand your own process. You might set a two- or three-year window for initial investments and review progress every six months, while retaining the freedom to slow down when suitable opportunities are scarce.

Diversification also has limits. Startup outcomes can be affected together when fundraising becomes difficult or buyers reduce spending. A portfolio of 20 does not guarantee a profit, and even a successful company can take a long time to return cash to investors.

blocks.text: 6. Use the same decision process for each deal

blocks.html: A portfolio plan is only useful if it informs the next decision. For each opportunity, return to the work from the previous lessons: screen against your thesis, carry out due diligence proportionate to the stage and understand the investment terms. Assess the founders' ability to execute, the size and accessibility of the market, product differentiation, evidence of customer demand, cash needs and plausible paths to scale. Treat forecasts as assumptions to test, not promises.
Then add the portfolio question: If I invest this amount, what does it do to my exposure, available reserves and future choices?
A short decision note can record:

• Why the company fits your thesis and what you believe it could become.
  • The two or three risks that could change your mind.
  • Your initial cheque and maximum exposure you would be comfortable taking later.
  • What evidence you would want to see before considering a follow-on.
  • Why this investment adds something to your existing portfolio.
It can be difficult to step back from a charismatic founder or a fast-moving round. Writing your reasons down gives you something to revisit when the next funding request arrives.

rows: What is my total budget, taking account of all high-risk holdings, and could I lose it?
What financial and wider aims guide my choices? Which sectors, stages and geographies fit?
How many companies could I realistically back, at what cheque size and minimum deal size?
How much will I keep available, and what evidence would justify using it?
Over what period will I make initial investments and review the plan?
What maximum exposure to one company or common risk am I comfortable with?
What due diligence, decision notes and portfolio updates will I maintain?

blocks.html: Final thought: You do not need a large portfolio or a perfect spreadsheet to start thinking like a portfolio investor. You do need a realistic budget, a repeatable decision process and the willingness to say no when a compelling individual deal does not fit the plan. The purpose of portfolio construction is to keep you able to make thoughtful decisions across many opportunities, including the ones you have not met yet.

blocks.text: How to stay informed and help the companies you back

blocks.html: Writing the cheque is the beginning of a new relationship. You have made an investment decision based on what a founder hopes to build and the evidence available at the time. From then on, you will learn whether customers want the product, whether the team can deliver and how much capital it takes to reach the next milestone.

As an angel investor, you can follow that progress, make better decisions about future rounds and sometimes help a company move forward. You might introduce its founder to a customer, share relevant experience or connect them with a specialist. The best support usually starts with a specific need raised by the company. It does not require you to manage the business.

This final lesson covers two connected activities: post-investment monitoring, which helps you understand what is happening across your portfolio, and value creation, which is the practical help you can offer when it is useful. Neither can guarantee a return. Both can make you a more informed, constructive investor.

blocks.text: 1. Know what information you can expect

blocks.html: Start with the investment documents and the route through which you invested. If you invested directly, check what reporting or information rights you were given. If you invested through a syndicate or special purpose vehicle (SPV), updates may reach you through its lead or manager. Some founders send detailed monthly reports; others provide brief quarterly updates. A small company will rarely have the reporting systems of an established business.
Before or soon after investing, find out:

• Who will send updates, how often, and where you can ask questions.
  • Which figures the company already tracks and can share reliably.
  • Whether you will hear about a new fundraising round directly or through a syndicate lead.
  • What information should remain confidential, including customer data and future fundraising plans.

An agreed communication cadence makes it easier for both sides to plan. Monthly written updates may suit a company moving quickly; quarterly updates may be more practical in other cases. Keep your requests proportionate to the size and stage of your investment. A consistent short update is more useful than a long report the founder cannot sustain.

If you hold shares through a nominee, SPV or syndicate, understand who speaks for investors and who can exercise any rights. A personal relationship with a founder does not necessarily give you direct rights to company information or decisions. Likewise, if you are offered an advisory or board role, agree its scope separately rather than assuming it comes with your investment.

blocks.text: 2. Track a few measures that tell you something useful

blocks.html: Key performance indicators (KPIs) are measures that help you assess progress against a company's own plan. They should reflect its business model and stage. A company still developing a product may focus on testing, user engagement and the time needed to reach a launch. One with paying customers may focus on revenue, repeat purchases and the cost of acquiring customers.

rows: Has the team delivered the product, customer, regulatory or hiring steps funded by the last round?
Are customers buying, returning and paying as expected? For subscriptions, monthly recurring revenue and churn may be useful.
How much cash remains, how quickly is it being spent and when might the company need more funding?
Are important roles filled? Have key people joined or left? Can the team act on what it learns?
What must be achieved before the next raise, and when does the company expect to start it?

blocks.html: Burn rate is the amount of cash a company spends each month, taking account of cash coming in. Runway is an estimate of how long its cash could last at that rate. For example, £600,000 in cash and a net burn of £50,000 a month suggest around 12 months of runway. That is only a snapshot: spending, receipts and one-off costs can change. Ask what assumptions sit behind the figure and when the company plans to raise, rather than treating the calculation as a deadline it can safely wait until.

Two other measures often appear in startup updates. Customer acquisition cost (CAC) estimates the cost of winning a customer. Customer lifetime value (CLTV) estimates the value a customer brings over the relationship. They can help test whether growth is sustainable, but early estimates may be based on very few customers. Likewise, a sales funnel shows how potential customers move from first contact to purchase; the important question is where people drop out and why.

Avoid comparing every company using the same set of numbers. A medical technology business awaiting a clinical milestone and a software company selling subscriptions will show progress in different ways. Choose a few measures that test the original investment case, then ask what has changed and what the founder has learned.

blocks.text: 3. Keep a simple record of your portfolio

blocks.html: You do not need sophisticated software to monitor a small angel portfolio. A spreadsheet can record the company, date and amount invested, instrument, investment terms, ownership where known, recent updates, cash runway where shared, next milestone and whether a decision is coming up. Save the company's updates and your own decision notes alongside it.

If you use a portfolio dashboard or specialist platform, check what data it actually receives and how often it is updated. A neat chart can make an old or uncertain figure look more precise than it is. Treat information provided by a founder, a syndicate lead and a public announcement as different kinds of evidence, and note the date of each.

One useful habit is to write down what you expected at the time of investing. If the company planned to reach ten paying customers, launch a pilot or secure a regulatory approval, future updates can be read against those commitments. A missed milestone does not automatically mean failure: the team may have found a better route. It does call for an explanation and a revised plan.
Review the portfolio periodically, perhaps every quarter or twice a year. For each company, ask:

• What has improved, weakened or stayed uncertain since my last review?
  • Does the company have enough cash to reach a meaningful next milestone?
  • Is there a useful introduction or piece of expertise I can offer?
  • Has anything changed that would affect my decision about a follow-on round?

This also gives you a way to report to anyone with whom you have agreed to share portfolio information, such as fellow syndicate members. Share only information you are permitted to disclose. Some company updates and financial figures are confidential.

blocks.text: 4. Respond to red flags with curiosity and discipline

blocks.html: Early-stage plans change. A product launch slips, a large customer delays signing, or growth costs more than expected. An isolated miss may be manageable. Several changes together, especially falling cash, missed milestones and unclear explanations, deserve closer attention.

Potential warning signs include repeated revenue shortfalls without a credible change in approach, rising burn with little evidence of customer demand, unexpected departures from the leadership team, or an upcoming raise that must happen before a useful milestone is reached. Long gaps in communication also matter, although silence alone does not tell you what has happened.

If a concern emerges, ask the founder or the relevant syndicate lead for context. What caused the change? What has the company learned? What actions are under way? What would make the plan credible again? Keep the conversation constructive and distinguish a difficult market from a problem the team can address. Do not assume you can fix a cash shortfall by making an introduction or writing another cheque.

As Lesson 5 discussed, a follow-on investment is a fresh decision. Revisit the original thesis, assess current evidence, read the proposed terms and consider your total exposure to the company. A lower valuation is not by itself a reason to refuse; a higher one is not proof of success. If the evidence no longer supports investing, you can decline even if you still want the founder to succeed.

blocks.text: 5. Offer help that fits the company's priorities

blocks.html: Money is only one contribution an angel can make. The value of your network or experience depends on whether it addresses a real need at the right time. Ask a founder what would help most over the next few months, then offer one or two things you can actually deliver.

Commercial support. You may know a potential customer or understand a buyer's decision process. A relevant introduction can help a founder test demand, learn how customers buy or open a sales conversation. Get permission from both sides and explain why the connection makes sense. You can also give feedback on a pitch to customers or on where prospects leave the sales funnel, while letting the company own its sales strategy.

Connections to people and capital. Introductions to strategic partners, specialist advisers or future investors can be valuable. Make them when the company's timing and materials are ready. An investor who works at a later stage may want to see evidence the company has not yet gathered. A thoughtful introduction with context is more useful than sending the founder a long list of names.

Strategic and technical perspective. If you know the sector, you may be able to test assumptions about market positioning, distribution, regulation or scaling. If you have relevant technical expertise, you can ask questions about a product roadmap or connect the team to someone better placed to assess it. State the limits of your knowledge. Advice grounded in yesterday's version of a market can be less useful than a founder's current customer evidence.

Organisation and hiring. As a startup grows, the founders may need clearer roles, better workflows and experienced leaders. You can share examples of how other teams have handled a transition or suggest candidates for a senior role. The company decides whom to hire and how to structure the team. A board, adviser or investor should also be alert to any personal interest in a proposed hire or service provider.

For some companies, long-term hiring plans may include share options or other equity compensation to attract and retain staff. Succession planning means preparing for leadership changes rather than relying on one person indefinitely. Both can matter as a business matures, but they are specialised decisions for the company and its advisers, not a standard task for every angel investor after a seed round.

blocks.text: 6. Be useful without adding work for the founder

blocks.html: Founders can receive advice from many investors, sometimes with conflicting opinions. Your aim is to help them make better decisions, not to create another reporting or approval process. Before offering support, consider whether the founder has asked for it, whether you have relevant experience and whether you can follow through.
Practical habits help:

1. Ask first. “Would an introduction to a procurement lead be useful now?” gives the founder an easy choice.
  2. Make the offer specific. Name the person, expertise or task you can help with and the likely time commitment.
  3. Close the loop. If you promise an introduction, make it; if it cannot happen, say so promptly.
  4. Respect boundaries. Do not contact customers, employees or prospective investors on the company's behalf without agreement.
  5. Accept a no. The founder may have priorities or information you do not see.

There may be periods when your most helpful action is to read the update, respond to a clear request and otherwise give the team space. You are invested in the outcome, but day-to-day decisions belong to the people running the company.

blocks.text: 7. Learn from the experience across your portfolio

blocks.html: Post-investment work can improve your next investment decision. Compare what you believed at entry with what happened later. Which risks did your due diligence identify? Which ones did you miss? Did a founder respond well when an assumption proved wrong? Were your introductions genuinely useful? Have you taken on more follow-on exposure than your portfolio plan allowed?

Do this without judging an early decision only by its eventual return. A strong process can still produce a loss; an unexpected gain does not prove every assumption was sound. Record the lesson and adjust your screening questions, investment notes or support commitments where the evidence calls for it.

Some investments may eventually return cash through an acquisition, a listing or a permitted sale of shares. Others may be written down or fail. Many may remain in the portfolio for years without a clear exit. Continuing to track them helps you understand both your financial exposure and the time you are spending as an investor. It also helps you decide where your attention can make a difference.

rows: Who sends them, how often, and what rights or arrangements support access?
Which two or three milestones and measures test the investment case?
What runway has been reported, on what date and with what assumptions?
What help has the founder requested, and what can I realistically deliver?
What evidence and terms would justify another investment within my portfolio limits?
Where will I keep updates, terms, decision notes and confidential information?

blocks.html: Final thought: Angel investing is a long relationship with uncertain outcomes. A good post-investment routine helps you notice what is changing, make deliberate decisions about further capital and support founders when your contribution is welcome. Across this series, the same discipline applies before and after the cheque: be clear about your thesis, test what you can, understand the risks and stay open to what the evidence teaches you.
